# ADR-0004: SBE codecs are generated by the reference's own sbe-tool

- Status: accepted (2026-10-05)

## Context

Five SBE schemas live in `schemas/`, and five things are generated from them:
the archive and cluster control protocols, the archive and cluster mark files,
and the cluster node-state file. Their ids and versions are byte contracts and
are recorded in `docs/compat.md`, not restated here. Nothing else in the system
is SBE — the UDP wire protocol, the CnC file, the counter files and the
cluster's `recording.log` are hand-written formats.

The tool that produces the reference's own codecs is
`uk.co.real-logic:sbe-tool`, pinned at 1.40.2 in the reference's
`gradle/libs.versions.toml`, driven by an XSD-validated `JavaExec` task. It
ships generators for Java, C, C++, C#, Go and **Rust**, all in the same jar.
Whether that Rust target existed was the open question this ADR had to
answer; it does, and everything below was measured rather than assumed.

**The Rust target works.** One invocation generates all five schemas. The
output is `#![forbid(unsafe_code)]`, declares no dependencies, and contains
no `Vec`, `String` or `Box` — zero allocation on both the encode and decode
paths.

**Its unit of output is a crate, not a file set.** It writes `Cargo.toml` +
`src/lib.rs` + one file per message. `lib.rs` holds the shared buffer
scaffolding (`ReadBuf`, `WriteBuf`, `SbeErr`, `Either` and four traits), and
every message file reaches for it with `use crate::*;`. So one schema yields
one self-contained crate, and the scaffolding is regenerated once per schema
— about 217 lines each, five times over. The generated code carries **no
"generated" banner**; nothing in it says it should not be hand-edited.

**There is no third-party Rust SBE generator worth depending on.** `sbe_gen`
(0.7.3) is the strongest of them and was measured: it does generate all five
schemas and compile, but its output allocates (287 `Vec` occurrences), it
pulls in `zerocopy`, and it repeats its error enums in 49 of its 52 files.
The crate named in the previous revision of this ADR, `sbe-rs`, does not
exist on crates.io.

**The reference's own answer to the same problem is to namespace it and
tolerate the duplication.** Its `generateCodecs` task emits both archive
schemas into one directory; `MessageHeaderDecoder` exists in
`io.aeron.archive.codecs` *and* `io.aeron.archive.codecs.mark`. Java does not
care, because each class is an independent compilation unit — there is no
crate root for the two copies to collide at. The C and C++ tasks do not even
generate the mark schema. The reference never writes a rewrite step over
generated code, in any language.

The reference's byte layout is the authority for this project. Generating
with the same tool from the same schema is what makes the golden fixtures
mean something: a byte mismatch then says *we* wired the generator up wrong,
rather than that two generators disagree.

## Decision

Use the reference's own `sbe-tool` 1.40.2, with `agrona` 2.6.1 on the
classpath, and `sbe.target.language=Rust`.

- **One crate per schema**, named as the generator names them:
  `io_aeron_archive_codecs`, `io_aeron_archive_codecs_mark`,
  `io_aeron_cluster_codecs`, `io_aeron_cluster_codecs_mark`,
  `io_aeron_cluster_codecs_node`. The names are kept because a name that
  says `io_aeron_...` is the clearest available marker that the code is
  generated, and it is what the Java side does too (it uses the schema's
  `package` name directly).
- **`Cargo.toml` is ours; `src/` is the generator's.** Each crate directory
  holds a hand-written manifest following the workspace conventions
  (`edition.workspace`, `license.workspace`, `[lints] workspace = true`) and
  a generated `src/` that regeneration overwrites wholesale. This is not a
  rewrite layer: nothing is edited, a whole directory is replaced.
- `deepmsg-codec` becomes a hand-written façade that re-exports the five.
- Generated sources are checked in. `build.rs` keeps validating schema
  presence and emitting rerun triggers; it does not generate. Regeneration
  is the explicit `just gen`, which:
  - locates the tool and pins its version (1.40.2 / 2.6.1),
  - **fails if the generator prints `[Error]`**,
  - runs `cargo fmt` over the result.
- Schemas are validated against the FIX `sbe.xsd`, copied verbatim into
  `schemas/fpl/`. The tool reports XSD violations but does not exit non-zero,
  so `just gen` greps for `[Error]` itself — the same check as above, which
  without it would be a log line nobody reads.
- Golden byte tests compare generated encoders against fixture bytes
  captured from the reference Java encoder, for every message template, plus
  round-trip decode tests.
- Decoding on the control channel must length-check before it wraps. The
  generated decoders index the buffer without validating it and have no
  error variant for "buffer too short"; the control channel is UDP, so a
  short datagram would otherwise panic a conductor thread. This is the
  caller's job, not the generated code's.

## Consequences

- Byte layout is inherited, not reverse-engineered. A golden mismatch is our
  bug — which is the property the whole archive test plan rests on.
- Encoders and decoders are allocation-free and unsafe-free without anyone
  here writing or auditing a generator.
- Regeneration needs a JDK and two jars, as a build-time dependency only.
  `cargo build` never invokes them, so offline builds still work.
- Five copies of the buffer scaffolding (~1,085 lines) sit in the tree.
  Cross-schema type sharing is not something we need — a control-protocol
  buffer and a mark-file buffer never meet — so the duplication is inert. It
  is the price of not owning a generator.
- The cluster schemas are carried and generated before the cluster track
  needs them, so the scaffolding stays uniform and the CI regeneration check
  covers them from the first day.
- Because the generated code carries no banner, "this is generated" is
  recorded by the directory, the ADR, and a line in each hand-written
  manifest. A reviewer who opens a `src/` file gets no warning from the file
  itself.
- Generated code is exempt from review judgement but not from the gates. It
  passes `clippy -D warnings` on its own `#![allow(clippy::all)]`, and it
  fails `cargo fmt --check` until `just gen` formats it — which is why that
  step is part of the recipe rather than a suggestion.
- We are tied to whatever this Rust target emits. It is the reference's own
  tool, but its Rust target is far less exercised than its Java one. The
  golden tests are what stand between us and a bad emission.
- The five SBE rows in `docs/compat.md` are claims until those golden tests
  land; the tests are what turn them into contracts. That is also why `just
  gen` is checked in CI rather than run by hand — a schema that drifted
  without its codecs following would otherwise keep the table looking
  verified.
